Simple regression and functional form

The audit supports further investigation. Operations now wants a simple planning relationship between a store’s usual delivery time and its stockout rate.

Business question → General theory → Worked application → Synthesis

First learn the definitions, notation, and logic of the method. Then use the shared case to work through the calculation and its interpretation.

Read here or present the same material, one step at a time.

The motivating question

Long delivery cycles are a plausible source of replenishment pressure. The analyst returns to the 150 baseline store profiles and asks how their average rates vary with usual delivery time. We will fit a straight line, trace several predictions and residuals, and decide what that relationship contributes to planning. This introduces regression through a question about familiar stores and a familiar outcome.

Define a regression and its fitted values

General theory

Simple regression represents the conditional mean with a line

Yᵢ = α + βXᵢ + uᵢ; fitted value Ŷᵢ = a + bXᵢ

Y is the outcome, X the predictor, α the population intercept, and β the population slope. The error u represents variation around the specified relationship. A linear conditional-mean interpretation uses E[u | X] = 0. The fitted coefficients a and b are estimates obtained from observed data.

An overall mean gives the same prediction to every observation. Group means give different predictions to categories; a fitted line summarizes a continuous relationship using an intercept and slope.

Ordinary least squares minimizes squared prediction misses

Choose a and b to minimize Σ[Yᵢ − (a + bXᵢ)]²

Each residual is the vertical difference between an observation and its fitted value. Squaring gives larger misses greater influence and makes the loss nonnegative. The fitted line is the one minimizing the sum over the estimation sample. This optimization defines OLS before any uncertainty or causal interpretation is added.

The slope measures outcome units per additional predictor unit

b = Cov(X,Y) / Var(X); a = Ȳ − bX̄

The slope is positive when X and Y move together and negative when they move in opposite directions. Its magnitude is expressed in units of Y per unit of X. The intercept supplies the fitted value at X=0. Read both coefficients against the units and range of the data.

Evaluate fit and choose a functional form

General theory

Residuals connect individual prediction misses with model fit

eᵢ = Yᵢ − Ŷᵢ; RMSE = √[Σeᵢ² / n]

A positive residual means the outcome exceeds its fitted value. Residual patterns can reveal systematic features missing from the chosen line. RMSE summarizes the squared misses in the original outcome units. On the estimation sample it describes training fit; performance on new observations requires separate evaluation.

R-squared describes the share of sample variation explained by OLS

SST = SSR + SSE; R² = 1 − SSE / SST

With an intercept, OLS partitions total squared variation around the sample mean into explained and residual components. SST is total variation, SSR explained variation, and SSE residual variation. R-squared is a relative measure of fit; RMSE reports an absolute error scale. Use both with the residual pattern.

Log transformations change the meaning of a slope

  • Level–level: one X unit corresponds to b Y units
  • Log–level: one X unit corresponds to approximately 100b% in Y
  • Level–log: 1% more X corresponds to approximately b/100 Y units
  • Log–log: 1% more X corresponds to approximately b% more Y

Choose a functional form from the relationship the model should express. Logs describe proportional changes and require positive values. The percentage interpretations are local approximations for small changes; exact finite changes use the log or exponential transformation. Compare predictions on a common outcome scale when assessing alternative forms.

Polynomial terms let the marginal association change with X

Ŷ = a + b₁X + b₂X²; slope at X = b₁ + 2b₂X

Read polynomial terms together through the predicted curve. The coefficient of X alone is not a constant slope once X² is included. Higher-order terms provide additional curvature. Plot the resulting predictions over the observed range and ask whether that flexibility captures a useful pattern.

Splines and local smoothing describe shape with different forms of flexibility

Linear spline: Ŷ = a + bX + c × max(X − knot, 0)

A linear spline changes the slope at a specified knot while keeping the curve continuous. Local smoothing instead fits relationships using nearby observations, often with distance-based weights. Both approaches help examine shape. Their tuning choices control how much detail the curve follows, so compare their implications on the same scale.

Put delivery time and the rate on the same row

Worked application

Worked application: Baseline profiles · weeks 1–8 · all 150 stores. Apply the general method to the shared retail records below.

Each row contains a store’s usual delivery time, measured in days, and its average stockout percentage over weeks 1–8. Longer lead time is a store characteristic; the outcome summarizes eight weeks of operations. We are studying the relationship across stores.

Start by grouping stores with the same delivery time and plotting their mean rates. This shows the shape before asking a fitted equation to summarize it. The observed delivery times range from two to five days.

Move from a group comparison to a fitted relationship

Worked application

Recover the slope from covariance

Slope = covariance(delivery days, rate) / variance(delivery days) = 1.62

The intercept is the mean outcome minus the slope times the mean predictor. These closed-form formulas describe simple regression with an intercept. A one-day slope is a difference in percentage points here, because the outcome itself is a percentage.

Fit a line and read its units

Worked application

The regression predicts a store’s baseline percentage as an intercept plus a slope multiplied by delivery days. Least squares chooses the two coefficients to minimize the sum of squared residuals. A residual is the actual rate minus the prediction for that store.

Predicted baseline rate (%) = 6.96 + 1.62 × delivery days

For a four-day delivery cycle: 6.96 + 1.62 × 4 = 13.43%

The slope is 1.62 percentage points per additional delivery day. It describes the fitted difference across these baseline stores. Its unit is a change in percentage points, rather than a percentage change in the stockout rate.

Trace fit through the stores it summarizes

Worked application

Five fitted store profiles

S00149.2013.43-4.24
S00239.0211.81-2.80
S003314.2011.812.38
S004514.6415.05-0.41
S005414.0213.430.58

The root-mean-square residual is 1.60 percentage points. It describes how far these baseline store averages typically sit from the fitted line, giving larger misses more influence. This is a fit summary for the data used to estimate the coefficients.

Several stores can have the same delivery time and different outcomes. Their demand, promotion schedules, location, and operating practices differ. The line compresses that variation into one planning relationship. Its simplicity makes the comparison easy to explain and also shows what the next analysis should add.

The director can use this relationship to anticipate which delivery patterns tend to come with more stockout pressure. Measuring the effect of changing a delivery process would require an intervention comparison. That question enters later through the alert policy.

Account for what the fitted line represents

Worked application

Partition the variation around the mean

OLS variation decomposition
QuantitySum of squares
Total: Σ(y − mean y)²854.61
Explained: Σ(fitted − mean y)²468.22
Residual: Σ(y − fitted)²386.39

Total = explained + residual; R² = 1 − residual / total

R² is 0.55. It describes how much of this sample’s variation is represented by the fitted relationship. It does not state the causal importance of delivery time or the accuracy of forecasts for later weeks.

Keep goodness of fit in business units

MSE = SSE / n = 2.58; RMSE = √MSE = 1.60 points

RMSE is easier to interpret than squared error because it returns to the outcome’s units. Here the divisor n describes average squared fitting error; a residual-variance estimate for inference uses the residual degrees of freedom instead. Read a model report in order: sample, outcome units, coefficients, uncertainty, then fit.

Let the operating relationship have a different shape

Worked application

Compare the forms on the same outcome scale

Level–level1.621.60

Models whose dependent variables are rate and log rate do not have directly comparable residual sums of squares on their fitted scales. The table evaluates predictions back in percentage points. Log-outcome predictions use a residual smearing factor when returning to the mean rate scale. Later validation asks how well a chosen procedure works on new observations.

Polynomial terms describe curvature jointly

Flexible delivery-time specifications
ModelCoefficients including interceptTraining RMSE
Linear21.60
Quadratic31.60
Cubic41.59
Spline, knot 3.531.60

A quadratic adds X²; a cubic adds X³. Interpret the predicted curve or its derivative, not the highest-order coefficient alone. Delivery time takes only four values in this case, so a cubic is already very flexible relative to the support. More training fit is a reason to validate, not a reason to extrapolate far beyond observed stores.

For each displayed demand value, fit a small weighted line using nearby stores, with closer observations receiving more weight. This LOWESS-style demonstration uses a 60% neighborhood and no robustness iterations. The bandwidth controls smoothness. It is an exploratory description of the same stores; the lab exposes its weighting rule.

Turn a simple relationship into a better question

Worked application

Use the fitted values as a rough benchmark for baseline store profiles within the observed two-to-five-day delivery range. Compare an unusually high residual with the store’s promotions and replenishment process. A residual can direct a useful conversation about what the one-variable model omitted.

The next lesson adds operating context to this same comparison. We will ask whether delivery time has the same fitted relationship in urban and other stores, and show how to calculate predictions for specified profiles.

Update the decision memo

Baseline stockout rates rise by about 1.62 percentage points per delivery day in the simple fitted comparison. Use the line to describe operating pressure and identify stores for review; next add the conditions that distinguish those stores.

Make the call

What is the difference between a positive residual and a positive delivery-time slope?

Compare your reasoning

A positive residual means a particular store’s actual rate is above its prediction. A positive slope means the fitted rate rises as delivery time rises across the comparison.

The bigger picture

A regression is a specified way to summarize how an outcome varies with predictors. The same reasoning applies to cost, demand, and performance relationships. Define the variables, choose the functional form, interpret its slope correctly, and inspect the residuals before deciding what the fitted relationship can contribute.

After your decision: open the known answer

The shared generator includes delivery time, location, demand, promotions, and store differences. The single-variable line summarizes their observed combination in the baseline profiles.
